title: Unit21 Alternatives: Replace It, or Add a Layer on Top
summary: Unit21 alternatives compared: replacement platforms such as Sardine, Flagright, Hummingbird and Hawk, plus Sphinx, a layer that clears alert work.
body_markdown:
**TL;DR:** Unit21 alternatives split into two groups: platforms that replace its monitoring and case management, and layers that do the investigation work while the tool stays where it is. Replacements fit teams whose detection or data model is the problem. A layer fits teams whose problem is the queue, which keeps growing as US filers send FinCEN 4.8 million SARs a year.


Sphinx wrote this list and appears on it, so read the first entry with that in mind. The vendors below were chosen because they either cover the same fraud, AML or case work as Unit21 or sit on top of it, and each was checked against its own public material in November 2026.


## What Unit21 does well, and what its agents actually do


Unit21 is a combined fraud and AML platform. Its public product line covers real-time fraud monitoring, AML transaction monitoring, sanctions and payment screening, case management, regulatory filing, customer risk rating, device intelligence and a fraud consortium. Teams that run fraud and AML together get one data model and one place to work, and the company reports that 5% of US SARs are filed through it.


Any comparison written before 2026 undersells it, because Unit21 has rebuilt around AI agents. The current product has two families. Detection agents, including a Rule Writer and a Rule Recommendation agent, study completed investigations and suggest rule changes. Investigation agents, split into Alert, Case and SAR agents, pull transaction histories, check watchlists, run open-source research, assemble evidence, recommend a disposition and draft a narrative in the customer's format.


Three details deserve a fair hearing. Unit21 says its agents generate SQL or Python to query data, so the model reasons while code executes, and every step lands in a work log. Autonomy is set per queue, use case and risk tier on a four-level ladder, from on-demand findings up to auto-close within guardrails. And in July 2026 Unit21 shipped Agentic Task Builder, which lets a compliance team describe a custom investigation task in plain English and backtest it against historical alerts before it goes live.


Unit21 also sells those agents as a bolt-on, running alongside another vendor's case management or detection stack. A team that is happy on Unit21 should test Unit21's own agents first. If they clear the queue, no second layer is needed.


## Replacing and layering solve different problems


The useful split is between detection and investigation. Detection decides what becomes an alert. Investigation decides what the alert means. A platform migration changes both, along with your rules, data feeds, case history and analyst habits. A layer changes only who does the first pass of the work.


Replacement makes sense when the problem sits in the detection engine or the data model: scenarios that miss your typologies, fraud signals you cannot get, a contract that no longer fits, or a sponsor bank asking for something the current tool does not produce. Layering makes sense when the alerts are fine and the people are stuck. Volume explains the pressure.[FinCEN's FY2025 Year in Review](https://www.fincen.gov/about-fincen/fincen-year-review) counts 4.8 million SARs filed, up from 4.3 million in FY2022, with 2.8 million from depository institutions and 1.26 million from money services businesses. Treasury has also pushed the other way on effort:[FinCEN's October 2025 SAR FAQs](https://www.fincen.gov/news/news-releases/fincen-issues-frequently-asked-questions-clarify-suspicious-activity-reporting) were issued so institutions could stop spending resources on low-value work and direct them at the most significant threats.


For the wider monitoring market, including rule engines and enterprise suites, see the[transaction monitoring software roundup](https://sphinxhq.com/blog-posts/best-transaction-monitoring-software-2026) .

## The list, in order of fit


The numbers below are an order of fit for a team on Unit21 deciding what to do next, not a quality ranking. Sphinx is first because it keeps the tool in place, with a login rather than a migration. The rest run from the closest match to Unit21's scope to the more specialized choices. Performance figures quoted for any vendor, Sphinx included, are that vendor's own.


### 1. Sphinx — Best for keeping your monitoring and case tool and clearing the alert work inside it


Sphinx sells AI compliance analysts that sign in to the tools a team already uses, the same way a new hire gets a user account. The[browser agents](https://sphinxhq.com/blog-posts/introducing-sphinx-browser-agents) open alerts, run KYC, KYB and AML checks, gather evidence and write case notes. Sphinx prepares the evidence, applies your SOPs, and produces a traceable recommendation; your team retains final approval. Sphinx reports 87% fewer false positives on average, a 3.2-minute median case and 94-98% agreement with analysts.[Alviere](https://sphinxhq.com/blog-posts/alviere-automates-86-of-compliance-cases-with-sphinx) went from 14 to 2.4 minutes per case.


The fit is a team whose rules are acceptable and whose queue is not, especially when one case crosses several systems. The limit is plain: Sphinx doesn't generate alerts. It has no rules engine, no watchlist data and no case tool of its own, so it cannot fix detection that misses risk. Pricing is a platform fee plus usage tiers scoped to your volumes.


### 2. Sardine — Best for fraud and AML on one platform with device and behavior signals


Sardine is the closest like-for-like replacement, since it also unifies fraud prevention, AML and real-time transaction monitoring. It adds a connections graph across users, devices and counterparties, a data consortium, a prebuilt AML rule library with backtesting, and case management. Its agent set covers sanctions and PEP screening, open-source research, graph analysis, rule writing and SAR narrative generation, with a no-code product called Sardine Flow tying data, rules, agents and human review together.


Sardine suits fintechs, merchants and banks where one risk team owns both fraud and AML, and where device and behavior context would change alert quality. The limit follows from the overlap: moving from Unit21 to Sardine is a full migration between two platforms with similar ambitions, so the case has to rest on a specific gap, such as signal depth, rather than on the concept.


### 3. Flagright — Best for monitoring and filing across many jurisdictions


Flagright combines real-time and post-transaction monitoring, dynamic risk scoring, watchlist screening, case management and regulatory filing, which it says reaches FinCEN and more than 70 goAML countries. Rule simulation and shadow rules let a team test changes before they go live. Its AI Forensics agents are built by uploading existing SOPs, then tested against historical cases and run in shadow mode, with reviewed recommendations as the next step and closing alerts on their own as the last.


Flagright suits fintechs, banks and credit unions that want rules and agents on one system, and the company says it can deploy in as little as two weeks. Two limits apply. The agents work inside Flagright's own case workflow, so getting them means moving onto the platform. And Flagright closed its Series A in June 2026, so a bank's third-party risk review will look closely at a vendor at that stage.


### 4. Hummingbird — Best for case and SAR work shared between analysts and agents


Hummingbird is built around investigations and regulatory reporting. In September 2026 it announced an agent orchestration platform: a shared workspace where its own agents, agents you build and third-party specialist agents work a case alongside analysts, with one record of everything that happened. Its Research and Review agents, released in June 2026, are also available over API, delivering output into an existing case management system. Monitoring runs on top of the customer's data warehouse.


Hummingbird suits teams that care most about case quality and filing, and that expect to run agents from more than one source. The limit is on the detection side. Hummingbird acquired Quantimon in October 2026 to bring machine learning into monitoring, and the announcement describes what customers can expect rather than what has shipped, so test today's monitoring against your scenarios.


### 5. Hawk — Best for banks that want explainable AI, as an overlay or a full platform


Hawk sells AML, screening and fraud, and it can be bought two ways. The full platform replaces monitoring and case management. The AML AI Overlay sits on an existing system and, according to Hawk, integrates regardless of vendor, scoring alerts and sending explanations back to your case manager. Its agent suite covers AML investigations, customer and payment screening, CDD and SAR preparation, and it offers SaaS or private cloud deployment.


Hawk suits banks and payment firms that want model governance material and deployment options to match. Two checks are worth making. The overlay requires sending customer and transaction data to Hawk through an integration layer, so it is lighter than a replacement but heavier than a login. Several agents are also new, with the CDD, Regulatory Reporting and Risk Exposure agents all launched between September and October 2026, so ask for production references agent by agent.


### 6. ComplyAdvantage Mesh — Best for screening-led programs that want data and workflow from one vendor


ComplyAdvantage Mesh is a cloud compliance platform built on the company's own risk database. It covers customer and company screening, transaction and payment screening, ongoing monitoring, risk scoring and case management, with agents for auto-remediation that the company says process 65-85% of profiles without human intervention. The differentiator is ownership of the data: sanctions and PEP changes arrive from its own intelligence rather than a third-party feed. In the interest of disclosure, Sphinx also connects natively to ComplyAdvantage.


Mesh suits teams whose biggest exposure is sanctions, PEP and adverse media, and who would rather buy data and workflow together. The limit comes from that focus. Mesh's public material leads with screening and risk data, so a Unit21 customer with heavy fraud monitoring or SAR volume should test those workflows directly before treating it as a full swap.


### 7. Feedzai — Best for larger programs that want ML alert prioritization across fraud and AML


Feedzai offers fraud and AML on one platform. Its AML product includes more than 20 out-of-the-box scenarios, self-service custom rules, a machine learning model that prioritizes alerts based on past alert, case and SAR outcomes, a case manager, and a SAR Manager for generating and e-filing reports. In September 2026 it launched Farol, an agent inside its RiskOps Studio that analyzes rule sets, retrieves case data, summarizes alerts and drafts SARs, and which A-Team Insight reports runs within each institution's environment.


Feedzai suits institutions with global fraud and AML programs that want to score and sequence alert work on a single platform. The limit is scope: A-Team Insight describes Farol as primarily aimed at fraud operations, so a team looking for an agent to work AML alerts end to end should ask exactly how far it goes today.


## Five questions that settle it


Most of this decision can be made with your own queue data, before any vendor call.


1. Where do your alerts go wrong? Pull 200 closed alerts and last year's escalations. If true risk is being missed or the noise is structural, look at detection and replacement. If the alerts are defensible and simply slow to work, a layer is the smaller change.
2. Have you run Unit21's own agents in parallel? They are the lowest-friction test available to a current customer. Measure them on your data before pricing anything else.
3. How many systems does one case touch? Agents built into a platform see that platform's data. If analysts also open a separate screening tool, a KYB provider or an internal admin panel for a typical case, check how each option reaches those systems. The[case management comparison](https://sphinxhq.com/blog-posts/best-compliance-case-management-software) goes further on this if the case tool itself is in question.
4. What does migration cost you, in full? Count rule rebuilds, parallel running, historical case access, retraining and the exam cycle you will be in when you cut over.
5. Who governs the agents?[SR 26-2](https://www.federalreserve.gov/supervisionreg/srletters/SR2602.htm) , which replaced SR 11-7 in April 2026, is expected to be most relevant to banks above $30 billion in assets and places generative and agentic AI models outside its scope, leaving appropriate controls to the institution's own risk management and governance. So every agent on this list sits under your governance. Ask each vendor what evidence it will give you for that file, and whether a person approves each outcome or only a sample.


Whichever path you take, run the shortlist against the same sample of real alerts and compare the written reasoning, not only the disposition. The vendor that can show its work on your hardest 50 cases will be easier to defend than the one with the better average. The[Sphinx AI Agents page](https://sphinxhq.com/products/ai-agents) shows how that work looks inside an existing stack.


## Frequently Asked Questions


### What is the best alternative to Unit21?


That depends on what you need changed. Sardine is the closest match for combined fraud and AML, Flagright and Hawk fit AML-led programs, and Hummingbird fits teams centered on cases and filing. If monitoring and case management are acceptable and the queue is the issue, a layer such as Sphinx avoids a migration.


### Does Unit21 have AI agents?


Yes. Unit21 offers investigation agents for alerts, cases and SAR narratives, plus detection agents that recommend and write rules. Autonomy is configurable per queue, use case and risk tier, and the Agentic Task Builder, launched in July 2026, lets teams build custom tasks in plain English.


### Can I keep Unit21 and add AI agents from another vendor?


Yes, though the routes differ. Sphinx signs in to existing tools the way an analyst does. Hawk says its overlay integrates with existing AML systems regardless of vendor, and Hummingbird delivers agent output into a current case system over API. Confirm any specific Unit21 setup with the vendor, including how outcomes get written back.


### How much does Unit21 cost?


Unit21 does not publish a price list, and buying starts with a demo. Sardine and Flagright also sell on quotes. Compare quotes on the same scope, because a screening or identity contract will look cheaper than a combined fraud and AML platform without doing the same job.


### Does Sphinx replace Unit21?


No. Sphinx doesn't generate alerts, maintain rules or hold watchlist data, so a team still needs detection and case management underneath it. Sphinx works the alerts those tools produce, prepares the evidence and produces a traceable recommendation, and the team retains final approval.
